title: Dasharatha's sacrifice
hook: a boy who had never seen another person, and the rain that followed him

segments.voice: Yesterday: Dasharatha's sacrifice, part one. A king with everything but a son, who asked his counselors before he acted. Did you tell someone what you've been carrying? Today, Sumantra's strange story. Day four hundred ninety-six.

Deep in a forest lives a sage, Vibhandaka, and his son, Rishyashringa. The boy has grown up with only his father, the trees, the sacred fire and the animals. He has never been to a town. He has never seen anyone but his father. Meanwhile, in the kingdom of Anga, a long way off, the rain has stopped. Fields crack. Wells sink. The king, Romapada, asks his priests what to do, and they give him an odd answer: bring the forest boy here, and the rain will come with him.
screen: `A BOY WHO'S ONLY SEEN HIS FATHER.` → `A KINGDOM WITHOUT RAIN.` → `BRING THE FOREST BOY.`

segments.voice: Here's how Sumantra tells it. The king's people can't just march in and take a sage's son. So they send young women from the city into the forest, with sweets and garlands. Rishyashringa, who has never met anyone, thinks they're young hermits from some other ashram, and he welcomes them with water and fruit, as a host should. They give him sweets he thinks are a new kind of fruit, and invite him to visit their hermitage. He goes with them, all the way to Anga, and the moment he enters the kingdom, the rain pours down. The king honors him and gives him his daughter, Shanta, in marriage. That's the story Sumantra brings to Dasharatha, who goes himself to Anga, to his old friend Romapada, and brings Rishyashringa and Shanta home to Ayodhya with great honor. Then the sacrifice. On the bank of the Sarayu, the horse is released to wander for a year, followed by guards, and when it returns the great rite is performed: altars of brick, priests from far kingdoms, gifts given away on an enormous scale. Why the rain story? Because it tells us who Rishyashringa is. A person so untouched, so simple and so full of tapas that the sky answers wherever he goes. The tradition says some blessings can't be taken by force. They have to be invited in.
screen: `THE KINGDOM OF ANGA, WITHOUT RAIN.` · `THE FOREST BOY IS INVITED OUT.` · `WHERE HE GOES, RAIN FOLLOWS.` · `THE HORSE IS RELEASED FOR A YEAR.` · then, large: `RISHYASHRINGA.`

segments.voice: Sit and settle, and imagine the first drops of rain on dry ground. That first smell. The dust darkening, the air cooling. Let your breath be like that rain, arriving without being forced. Each breath in, a little water on dry earth. Each breath out, the ground soaking it in. Nothing to make happen. Just let it come. The bell holds the time.
Dasharatha's sacrifice. To perform it, the king brings Rishyashringa, the forest sage whose coming brought rain to a dry kingdom, to Ayodhya.
Your line: Dasharatha's sacrifice. Today, instead of pushing for something you want, invite it: one gentle ask, one open door, and then let it come or not. Day four hundred ninety-six.

howItsDone: Rishyashringa is honored in several local temple traditions in India, and his story is told as part of the Ramayana's opening, usually as the reason the rain-bringing sage leads Dasharatha's rites.

myth: Rishyashringa had grown up seeing only his father
so he took the visitors for young hermits.
Rishyashringa is taken to Anga by force
he is invited, and goes willingly, and the rain follows him.
the horse wanders for a year before the sacrifice
released on the Sarayu's bank, followed by guards.

fork.setup: you're the king of Anga. a holy boy in the forest can end your drought, but his father would never let him go. what do you do?
options: send people to befriend him and invite him.
wait for the rain on your own.
fork.reveal: he sends visitors with gifts who invite the boy out. Rishyashringa comes, the rain falls, and he marries the king's daughter.

original.note: Sanskrit ṛśyaśṛṅga: deer-horned, from ṛśya, a kind of antelope, and śṛṅga, horn.

trapdoor: what you thought: a side story before the real one starts.
what it means: it shows who the sage is, someone the sky answers, and why he must be invited, not taken.

what a scholar hears: the Rishyashringa episode is also told in the Mahabharata's Vana Parva; in Valmiki's southern recension Shanta is Romapada's daughter, while some later tellings make her Dasharatha's daughter adopted by Romapada.

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Bala Kanda 9–11 (Rishyashringa, Anga, Shanta)
Valmiki Ramayana, Bala Kanda 12–14 (the horse sacrifice on the Sarayu)

notes: Shanta's parentage differs between recensions and later tellings; stated with that caveat in the trapdoor. Confirm.
The women sent into the forest are courtesans in the text; the script says 'young women from the city'. Keeper may prefer the text's word.
howItsDone mentions local temple traditions honoring Rishyashringa without naming one (e.g. Kigga near Sringeri); a Keeper may want to name one.
